title: Why the Bronze Age Collapsed
author: AnodicElegy
tldr: Patrick Fitzsimmons argues that iron kept Bronze Age empires from coming back after they fell around 1200 BC. Bronze needed tin from a few distant mines, and only big states could get it reliably. Iron ore is common almost everywhere. Once villages could make their own weapons, no state could hold a large empire for centuries.

keyPoints: Droughts, invaders and revolts can explain why the empires fell around 1200 BC. Fitzsimmons asks a different question: why nothing like them returned for centuries.

Bronze needs tin, and the main tin deposits were in Afghanistan, France, Iberia and Cornwall. Tin reached the Syrian city of Mari from Elam, 500 miles away, and Elam got it from mines another 1,000 miles off.
Scarce tin gave large states an edge in weapons. They could secure trade routes, build stockpiles and replace losses better than small rivals.

Bloomery furnaces reached 1,200 to 1,300 degrees Celsius, which was enough to pull iron out of ore without melting it. Iron is not better than bronze. Its ores are common and easy to spot, so local smiths could arm the periphery.

Fitzsimmons cites several kinds of evidence. No early Iron Age empire matched its Bronze Age predecessors in size. Skeletons show more violence, and Fitzsimmons's battle database shows more battles in the century after a region adopted iron. Average reigns in Assyria, Babylon and Athens got 29 percent shorter.

Fitzsimmons compares iron to modern drones, which cost a few hundred dollars and can threaten a tank. The essay also compares AI providers, who can cut off access, to Bronze Age kings who controlled tin.
article.whyItMatters: Read the original for the metallurgy and the ancient sources. It explains how a bloomery works and why iron ores were easy to find. It also quotes Hesiod, Herodotus and Lucretius on iron making war cheaper. The reign-length and battle data are Fitzsimmons's own work, and the essay admits their limits.

comments.overview: The thread was large and mostly skeptical. The biggest argument was not about the Bronze Age at all. It was about one image caption claiming Spanish steel beat the Aztecs. On the main thesis, commenters said the timeline is backwards, because iron spread after the collapse, not before it.

themes.title: Did Spanish weapons beat the Aztecs?
themes.synthesis: The top comment attacked the article's caption, saying Cortés won through native allies, not steel. Others answered that steel armor, horses and cavalry made the Spanish nearly invincible in open battle, and that this won them the allies in the first place. A third camp said tactics and veteran soldiers mattered more than any object they carried. Smallpox came up often, with disagreement over whether it decided the war or arrived too late to matter.

quotes.author: beloch
quotes.text: So, yes, the Spanish won allies who helped them fight the Mexica, but they needed their guns, steel, and horses to win those allies.

quotes.author: CSMastermind
quotes.text: Cortez won primarily because he had an army with a nucleus of veterans from the Italian wars that applied the lessons of the Reconquista.

themes.title: The timeline runs the other way
themes.synthesis: Many commenters said iron working spread only after the empires fell. In their view the collapse cut off the tin trade, and smiths turned to iron because bronze was gone. Defenders replied that the article only claims iron prevented recovery, not that it caused the fall. Critics then asked how the Assyrians, Persians and Romans built huge empires in the Iron Age if iron keeps power spread out.

quotes.author: netcan
quotes.text: So... Causation seems to be backwards. Bronze production mostly ends. Iron working starts gradually expanding in the absence of bronze.

quotes.author: falaki
quotes.text: If true why and how were Assyrians and Persians able to build such large empires long after iron weapons were wide spread?

themes.title: How good was early iron?
themes.synthesis: Commenters argued over what early iron was like. One said it was brittle like modern pig iron. Others corrected this. Bloomeries made soft, low-carbon wrought iron, and smiths added carbon to the surface later. Some said iron allowed longer, lighter blades than bronze. Others said real steel stayed rare until the Roman era or later.

quotes.author: imtringued
quotes.text: Hence primitive wrought iron came first and because it had low carbon it was highly malleable.

quotes.author: mr_toad
quotes.text: Compare the profile of bronze age and iron age swords in any museum and you can see that the bronze blades are shorter and wider that the iron weapons, and they would be considerably heavier.

themes.title: What actually caused the collapse
themes.synthesis: Several commenters pointed to Eric Cline's systems-collapse view, where many shocks hit at once. Some said the palace economies were so unequal that common people welcomed the invaders. Others described the Sea Peoples as refugees from drought or war. One commenter challenged the whole picture of widespread destruction, citing a study that rejected most claimed destruction sites. A side debate asked whether the collapse was good for ordinary people or simply a disaster.

quotes.author: cobbzilla
quotes.text: But you don’t get the wholesale overthrow of so many empires without the common people being at least somewhat welcoming of the invaders (when not happily assisting them!) in throwing off centuries of elite oppression.

quotes.author: db48x
quotes.text: Jesse Millek examines 153 sites claimed to have been destroyed and found that 61% never happened, happened during a different time period, or had a different cause.

themes.title: Tests of the tin argument
themes.synthesis: One commenter offered the Harappan civilization as a counterexample, since it had bronze but little sign of central power. Others replied that Harappan tin was local, so it fits the theory. Another commenter asked why the first people to master iron did not simply conquer everyone. The answer was that iron skills could spread to any rival, while bronze needed tin that most people could not get.

quotes.author: GMoromisato
quotes.text: In an area where tin is abundant, individuals could easily forge their own bronze weapons, thus making it harder for the state to have a monopoly on high-tech weapons.

quotes.author: bluGill
quotes.text: Bronze it wouldn't matter because I can't get the raw materials anywhere, and so I can't create an army to oppose you.

comments.consensus: Most commenters agreed the collapse had several causes. They doubted that iron explains it alone, and they saw iron mainly as a result of the lost tin trade.
comments.dissent: A minority defended the thesis. They said the article explains why empires did not return, not why they fell, and that cheap local weapons made it costly for any king to rebuild.

contrarian.author: cucumber3732842
contrarian.text: You can't "just regulate the smiths" like some 21st century despot because those smiths also make the iron tools those people need to farm to pay your taxes.
contrarian.why: Critics asked why a pharaoh could not crush rebels and seize the smelters, and this comment gives the economic reason why not.
